newsitem.title: USA: N.J. pension bond sale under legal assault.
newsitem.headline: N.J. pension bond sale under legal assault.

text.p: Mere hours after Gov. Christie Whitman put her signature on the pension bond law at midnight, a state judge Friday heard arguments that it was unconstitutional.

Superior Court Phillip S. Carchman promised to rule Monday or Tuesday on whether the state can raise $2.75 billion to liquidate state unfunded pension obligations by selling bonds -- without obtaining voter approval in a referendum.

Alan J. Karcher, a lawyer for Mayor George Spadoro of Edison Township, argued that the proposal does not meet two criteria the state Supreme Court laid out for exceptions to the state constitution's debt limitation clause.

The pension bond plan does not build a tangible asset, as did state bonds financing the Meadowlands sports complex,he said. And it is not supported by an income stream, such as a race track or toll road produces.

Instead the pension bond law authorizes the state treasurer to contract with the nominally independent Economic Development Authority to sell the bonds in return for the pledge to pay the debt service from annual appropriations. It also helps balance the annual budget.
Whitman signed it into law late Thursday night.

Her original pension bond plan was to borrow $3.4 billion enabling her to forgo $647 million in contributions to the state's four funds. The state Senate pared it and reduced its budget benefit to $590 million.
"It's all a sham. It's all a game. It's a trick ... to get you to thumb your nose at the Constitution," Karcher told the judge.
The plan creates a moral and practical obligation on the state, but not a constitutional one, Assistant Attorney General Jaynee LaVecchia replied.
"The Legislature has said quite clearly it is not attempting to bind future Legislatures," she said. "It is subject to annual appropriations.
"Bondholders will purchase with notice of that risk." ((--U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650))
